lines.text: Do you know how volcanoes work? Deep under your feet, Earth is hot enough to melt rock.
Earth's outer shell is broken into giant plates. They move a few centimeters a year, about as fast as your fingernails grow.
Where one plate dives under another, it drags water down with it. That water lowers the melting point of the hot rock above, so it melts into magma.
Magma is lighter than the solid rock around it, so it rises, and collects in a chamber a few kilometers below the surface.
It's full of dissolved gas, like water vapour and carbon dioxide. As it rises, the pressure drops, and the gas forms bubbles, like opening a shaken soda.
When the pressure gets too high, it bursts through. Runny magma pours out as lava, around a thousand degrees Celsius. Sticky magma traps the gas, and explodes into ash.
That's why most volcanoes sit where plates meet. The Pacific Ring of Fire has about four hundred and fifty of them.
So every volcano is Earth, letting out its heat.
